title: Bias in AI
lines: Bias in AI explains why fairness problems cannot be reduced to biased training data.
Its course follows harmful pathways through measurement, language models, retrieval, and agent decisions.
The central lesson is to identify what is distorted before choosing a metric.
Different fairness criteria protect different interests and can conflict.
Readers learn to examine consequential dependencies without expecting one universal fairness score.

title: Different paths, similar answers
lines: Two matched users can receive similar final answers after very different agent journeys.
One may receive additional research, a tool call, or escalation to a human.
The other may receive none of those resources.
The book treats those choices as allocations that ordinary text benchmarks can miss.
That example explains why its account extends from model behavior to complete workflows.

title: Name what the measure protects
lines: A predictive target can reflect an institution's assumptions rather than the outcome people actually need.
Different fairness criteria also protect different interests, and some cannot hold together.
The book asks readers to identify the population, harm, measurement, and decision context.
A good score cannot settle the institution's responsibility for choosing those standards.
This distinction connects technical analysis with visible ownership of normative decisions.

title: Read beyond the bias score
lines: Start with the distinctions between statistical bias, harmful disparities, and normative disagreement.
Then follow how retrieval, memory, and agents create additional pathways to unequal outcomes.
The final chapters examine evidence that must be renewed after system changes.
Bias in AI is useful because it keeps the object of evaluation explicit.
Read it to investigate particular harmful dependencies and judge whether a proposed intervention addresses them.
